title: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
content: Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides. Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls. Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised. That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group. Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain. Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes. Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment. "This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says. Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin. Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer. Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain. Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago. Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease. Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died. Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025. Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner. Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico. Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises. But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild. Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands". Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales. "If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement. In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs". Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care". They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well. World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project. As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales. "I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds. The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m). But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales. One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer. "They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks. "It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild. Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws, and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity. Jason Jones, senior curator of animal well-being at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life". "Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so." Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, 7. They joined the four females already in their care. They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says. "There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group." "They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then." Phil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who the BBC spoke to, said the end of Marineland is "bittersweet". He's grateful to see the facility shut down, and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat. He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV. "I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says. A Sowerby's beaked whale is seen by passengers on a ferry. Sir David says the series uncovers marine life that is "even more precious than we ever realised". The men are accused of stealing around 2,700 cats in Ho Chi Minh City, allegedly to be slaughtered for food. Conservationists say the animal was discovered on a Cornish beach during an event. Wildlife cameraman Dan Abbot is caught off guard by a humpback whale, a rare sight in Welsh waters. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
content: German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death. The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death. The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates. Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime. The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K. He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday. According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country. He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims. Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency. While his extradition was first reported in early October , the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations. Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab. A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere. King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly" . A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result". "The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time. A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died. It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack. Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death. In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption. The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom. The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid. At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine . But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for. The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations. It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025. It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests. Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here . NHS leaders hope to be handed the keys to the new centre in December. 1,500 people have signed with some saying they missed loved one's deaths due to parking issues. People can view the latest designs and proposals for the new hospital, including a scale model. The trust that runs hospitals in Colchester and Ipswich says it accepts the findings of a report. South Central Ambulance Service is applying to partially rebuild its hub in High Wycombe. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
content: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history. Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband. There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel. In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage. Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children. There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year. Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire. Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark. They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others. The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment. Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car. On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands. The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg. Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention. Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting. All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation. The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children. Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him. In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed. A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back. In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending. He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her. She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative. She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that. The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation. Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them." The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022. Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case. However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation. Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded". Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months. The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court. The man, a Mexican firefighter, looked "nervous" as he tried to leave Cologne Airport, officials say. Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines. Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was committed to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe". David Rush, who also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, had revealed the existence of a "clandestine human source", prosecutors said. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
